Abstract 
Longitudinal cracking poses a serious threat to the longevity and functionality of con‑
tinuously reinforced concrete pavement (CRCP). Using structural, traffic, and climatic 
data taken from the Long-Term Pavement Performance (LTPP) database, this study 
presents a machine learning system based on a gradient boosting machine (GBM) 
optimized using particle swarm optimization (PSO) to forecast longitudinal cracking. 
The proposed PSO-GBM model achieved the lowest mean RMSE (2.661) and highest R2 
(0.984) across fivefold cross-validation, outperforming baseline GBM, linear regression, 
random forest, artificial neural networks (ANN), and support vector regression (SVR). 
Compared to traditional and untuned models, the PSO-GBM offers improved generali‑
zation and a stronger ability to capture nonlinear interactions among variables. Feature 
importance and sensitivity analyses identified L3 thickness, age, and AADTT as key pre‑
dictors. Despite the model’s exceptional predictive accuracy, computational demands 
and data availability may limit its practical application. However, the results offer useful 
information for transportation organizations looking to improve maintenance planning 
techniques and incorporate intelligent predictive tools into pavement management 
systems.
Keywords:  Longitudinal cracking, Concrete pavement, Particle swarm optimization, 
Gradient boosting machine, Hybrid machine learning, Pavement management systems
Introduction
One of the prominent distress types found in continuously reinforced concrete pavement 
(CRCP) is longitudinal cracking [1, 2]. These cracks are indicative of serious structural 
issues with the pavement system and usually happen parallel to the pavement centerline 
[3, 4]. Thermal stresses caused by temperature changes, shrinkage, cyclic traffic loading, 
and material aging are some of the reasons for longitudinal cracking [5]. If left unre-
paired, these cracks can permit water into pavement layers, speeding up subgrade ero-
sion, compromising structural strength, and eventually decreasing pavement lifespan 
[6]. Thus, fixing longitudinal cracking is vital to ensure CRCP’s durability, safety, and 
serviceability [7]. However, because of complexity and variability of causative factors,

pavement engineering continues to face significant challenges in accurately predicting 
longitudinal cracking and its early detection [8, 9].
A key component of efficient pavement management systems (PMS) is the ability to 
accurately forecast longitudinal cracking [10, 11]. Transportation authorities may effec-
tively manage resources, prioritize maintenance tasks, and create rehabilitation plans 
that are suited to the unique circumstances of each site by using prediction models [12, 
13]. Traditionally, such forecasts relied on regression-based statistical models [14]. Nev-
ertheless, these models frequently have limitations when it comes to managing multi-
collinearity and nonlinear interactions among the many elements affecting pavement 
performance [15]. The increasing complexity of modern road networks and the avail-
ability of large datasets have created a growing demand for advanced modeling tools that 
can capture interactions among traffic, environment, and materials [16].
Machine learning (ML) has emerged as an effective alternative to predictive modeling 
in pavement engineering [17–19]. ML algorithms outperform standard statistical meth-
ods in capturing complicated, nonlinear patterns in high-dimensional datasets [20–22]. 
Among these strategies, gradient boosting machine (GBM) has been particularly use-
ful in tackling engineering challenges because to its capacity to merge numerous weak 
learners into a strong predictive model [23]. GBM has been successfully used in a variety 
of pavement engineering projects, proving its ability to model complex relationships and 
enhance forecast accuracy [24]. However, its performance is heavily reliant on hyperpa-
rameter selection, such as the learning rate, number of learning cycles, and maximum 
depth of decision trees [25]. Improperly tuned hyperparameters can lead to overfitting 
or underfitting, reducing the model’s predictive reliability.
Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a population-based optimization algorithm 
inspired by the social behavior of swarms, such as fish schools or birds flocking [26, 27]. 
PSO systematically explores the hyperparameter space in an effort to minimize a defined 
objective function, such as root mean square error (RMSE). By combining PSO with 
GBM, the resulting PSO-GBM hybrid model can achieve enhanced predictive perfor-
mance and robustness. This hybrid approach has shown promise in various fields and 
offers significant potential for advancing predictive modeling in pavement engineering.
A well-known worldwide source of high-quality, standardized pavement performance 
data is the Long-Term Pavement Performance (LTPP) database [28, 29]. The LTPP data-
base, which was created as a component of the Strategic Highway Research Program, 
has comprehensive records on pavement performance indicators, traffic loads, weather, 
and structural features [11]. Pavement engineering research benefits greatly from this 
abundance of data as it enables researchers to create and verify prediction models 
under a variety of real-world conditions. Thirty-three CRCP sections and 395 observa-
tions, spanning a broad variety of climatic, structural, and traffic circumstances, were 
extracted from the LTPP database for this study.

LTPP database. The reviewed studies covered a broad spectrum of distresses, includ-
ing faulting, spalling, International Roughness Index (IRI), and transverse crack-
ing, across different rigid pavement types such as jointed plain concrete pavement

learning models were explored—ranging from traditional approaches like linear 
regression and decision trees to advanced ensemble models (XGBoost, AdaBoost, 
CatBoost), neural networks, and optimization-based hybrids like SVR with genetic 
algorithm (GA) and XGBoost tuned by Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE). 
Across most studies, ensemble methods and optimized kernel models consistently 
outperformed baseline models in terms of R2 and RMSE, demonstrating their supe-
rior ability to capture complex non-linear relationships in pavement deterioration 
data. Additionally, many studies emphasized the importance of feature selection, 
interpretability (e.g., SHAP analysis), and data preprocessing. The inclusion of traffic 
loads (AADTT, KESAL), climate indices (freeze index, precipitation), and structural 
parameters (layer thickness, age, IRI) as input variables was recurrent, highlighting 
their critical role in distress prediction. This table not only contextualizes the cur-
rent study but also underscores the novelty of integrating PSO-optimized GBM for 
longitudinal cracking prediction in CRCP, a relatively underexplored distress in the 
existing literature.
While many studies have explored the use of machine learning in pavement mod-
eling, limited research has addressed longitudinal cracking in CRCP using hybrid 
optimization models. Several transportation agencies, however, have begun adopt-
ing predictive models to inform maintenance strategies. Several US transportation 
agencies have adopted predictive modeling to support maintenance planning and 
resource allocation. For instance, the North Carolina Department of Transporta-
tion (NCDoT) is actively exploring predictive models across its 79,000-mile road 
network to conduct cost–benefit analyses and optimize maintenance strategies [37]. 
Their approach involves developing separate deterioration models for individual 
pavement distresses, assigning weights, and calibrating coefficients using annual 
performance monitoring data. Likewise, the Indiana Department of Transportation 
(IDOT) implements a Pavement Condition Index (PCI) framework that incorporates 
dedicated prediction models for key distresses such as cracking, rutting, roughness, 
faulting, and friction, each weighted based on its contribution to overall pavement 
condition [38]. While these implementations primarily rely on regression-based 
approaches, they illustrate how agencies can operationalize predictive modeling to 
inform pavement management decisions.
This study aims to develop and evaluate a robust hybrid machine learning model, 
combining PSO with GBM, for predicting longitudinal cracking in CRCP using data 
from the LTPP database. The research benchmarks the performance of the PSO-
GBM model against baseline GBM, linear regression, random forest, artificial neu-
ral networks (ANN), and support vector regression (SVR) models using metrics 
such as RMSE and R2 to demonstrate its superiority. Feature importance and sen-
sitivity analyses are conducted to identify key predictors and evaluate the impact 
of hyperparameters and input variables on predictions. The model’s reliability is 
validated using k-fold cross-validation, and practical recommendations are provided 
for enhancing pavement maintenance and management strategies. By leveraging 
advanced machine learning techniques, this study contributes to improving predic-
tive capabilities in PMS and offers actionable insights for the maintenance and man-
agement of CRCP.

Methods
Data description
The LTPP database, a widely used and internationally recognized resource for pave-
ment performance research, provided the data for this study. The dataset consists of 
395 observations from 33 CRCP sections that were chosen to capture a variety of traf-
fic, structural, and climatic conditions. The length of longitudinal cracking, expressed 
in meters, is the analysis’s target variable. This is a crucial sign of pavement distress that 
affects the CRCP’s functionality and longevity.
Twenty independent variable total, divided into four categories—structural, climatic, 
traffic, and performance-related factors—are included in the dataset. All of these fac-
tors have a major impact on longitudinal cracking. The following structural variables 
have either numeric or categorical values: age (years), construction number, kinds and 
thicknesses of pavement layers (#2, #3, and #4), and overall pavement thickness. Cli-
mate zone, a categorical variable with four different classifications—dry freeze, dry non-
freeze, wet freeze, and wet non-freeze—is one of the climatic variables. These categories 
ensure that the dataset includes a diverse variety of environmental circumstances, allow-
ing the model to generalize across different geographical regions. Other environmental 
characteristics accounted for in the model include yearly average precipitation (mm), 
annual average temperature (°C), annual average freeze index (°C-degree days), and low-
est and maximum relative humidity (percentages). Traffic-related factors include the 
number of lanes (categorical), equivalent single axle loads (ESALs), annual average daily 
traffic (AADT), and annual average daily truck traffic (AADTT), which are all numeri-
cal. The performance-related variable, the initial International Roughness Index (IRI, m/
km), is similarly numerical.
For the purpose of modeling longitudinal cracking, these variables offer a thorough 
understanding of the pavements’ structural, environmental, traffic-related, and per-
formance components. These characteristics are compiled and categorized as either 
numeric or categorical in Table 2.
Figure 1 shows the geographic distribution of the 33 selected CRCP sections analyzed 
in this study. These sections are located across various regions of the USA, encompass-
ing a wide range of climate zones, structural designs, and traffic conditions. According 
to the LTPP database, 13 of these sections are classified as active, while 20 are desig-
nated as out-of-study. This diverse geographic spread enhances the dataset’s applicabil-
ity, supporting the development and validation of robust machine learning models for 
predicting longitudinal cracking under varied real-world conditions. The map highlights 
the dataset’s extensive coverage, spanning states from the northeast to the southwest, 
thereby capturing a broad spectrum of environmental and operational contexts.

To enhance the reproducibility and transparency of this study, additional details 
regarding the structural configuration of the analyzed CRCP sections are provided. Each 
section was modeled as a four-layer pavement system consisting of:
1.	 a subgrade (layer 1),
2.	 a subbase layer (layer 2),
3.	 a base layer (layer 3), and
4.	 a concrete surface layer (layer 4).
These layers represent a typical CRCP structural composition consistent with real-
world construction practices documented in the LTPP database. The types of materials 
used in each layer were classified using standardized LTPP codes. The subgrade layer 
(L1) generally comprised untreated soil (classified as SS), the subbase (L2) included 
unbound granular subbase (GS) or treated subbase (TS), and the base layer (L3) was 
primarily composed of bound or unbound base materials such as granular base (GB) 
or treated base (TB). The surface layer (L4) was consistently Portland cement concrete 
(PC), reflecting the defining characteristics of CRCP.
Each layer’s type was encoded numerically for machine learning purposes using the 
LTPP’s classification system (e.g., PC as 2, SS as 7). These standardized codes ensured 
uniform representation of material categories across all observations. Additionally, 
structural layer thicknesses were included for layers 2 through 4, and the total pave-
ment thickness was incorporated as a numerical input feature. Although detailed mate-
rial properties such as elastic modulus or Poisson’s ratio were not explicitly available in 
the dataset, the use of recognized LTPP classifications and thickness measurements sup-
ports both the consistency and reproducibility of the structural inputs.
To guarantee the quality and preparedness of the dataset for the creation of machine 
learning models, the data preprocessing stage was essential. Twenty independent vari-
ables and one target variable that represented the degree of longitudinal cracking in 
CRCP made up the dataset, which was taken from the LTPP database. The dataset may 
still contain biases related to geography or design, even though it captures a variety of 
traffic, structural, and environmental conditions across different US regions. Handling 
missing values, encoding categorical variables, normalizing continuous variables, con-
trolling outliers, and getting the data ready for training and validation were all examples 
of preprocessing steps.
To assure the analysis’s consistency and quality, a number of data pretreatment meas-
ures were taken. The dataset has few missing values due to the standardized nature of 
the LTPP database; any missing items were evaluated and imputed using appropriate 
statistical methods to maintain integrity. Categorical variables, such as climate zones 
and pavement layer kinds, were numerically represented to make them more useful in 
machine learning models. For example, climate zones were encoded with numerical

Alnaqbi et al. Journal of Engineering and Applied Science           (2025) 72:58 
	
values (1 for “Wet, Freeze,” 2 for “Wet, Non-Freeze,” 3 for “Dry, Freeze,” and 4 for “Dry, 
Non-Freeze”). Similarly, pavement layer types were assigned numerical values ranging 
from 1 to 8, ensuring interpretability while avoiding arbitrary ordinal assumptions.
Continuous variables were normalized using z-score normalization to guarantee equi-
table contribution to the model. This technique changed each variable’s mean to zero 
and standard deviation to one, preventing variables on bigger scales, such as annual 
average daily traffic (AADT) and annual average daily truck traffic (AADTT), from sub-
stantially impacting the model’s performance. Normalization ensured a balanced scale 
across all predictors, which strengthened the training process.
Using the interquartile range (IQR) rule, values that were more than 1.5 times the IQR 
above the third quartile or below the first quartile were flagged as outliers. To enhance 
the quality of the data, unrealistic or incorrect outliers were eliminated, but true extreme 
values were kept to represent actual circumstances. By taking into consideration a vari-
ety of field situations, this method improved the model’s generalizability.
Fivefold cross-validation was used to separate the dataset into training and testing 
subsets in order to verify the model’s dependability and avoid overfitting. This method 
gave a reliable estimate of the model’s performance on unseen data by ensuring that it 
was trained and assessed on various data subsets. Descriptive statistics were recalcu-
lated after preprocessing to ensure the dataset was prepared for machine learning 
applications.
Using these rigorous pretreatment methods, the dataset was thoroughly cleaned, nor-
malized, and structured for predictive modeling. This ensured that the methodology was 
reliable and resilient, allowing for accurate prediction of longitudinal cracking in CRCP 
under a variety of situations.
Model development
The primary objective of this study was to develop and assess machine learning mod-
els for predicting longitudinal cracking in CRCP. Three models were designed and com-
pared: a PSO-optimized gradient boosting machine (PSO-GBM), a baseline GBM, and a 
linear regression model. These models were chosen to represent a range of complexity, 
interpretability, and predictive capabilities. The methodology for developing these mod-
els is detailed as follows:
GA‑GBM
The PSO-GBM is an advanced predictive modeling approach that combines the GBM 
algorithm with the hyperparameter optimization capabilities of PSO. This hybrid 
approach enhances the accuracy and robustness of predictions by systematically opti-
mizing critical hyperparameters in the GBM model. Below, we detail the methodology, 
equations, and steps involved in developing the PSO-GBM model.
GBM is an ensemble learning method that combines the predictions of multiple weak 
learners, typically decision trees, to build a strong predictive model. The GBM algorithm 
minimizes a differentiable loss function L(y,ŷ) by sequentially adding decision trees, 
where each tree corrects the residual errors of the previous ensemble. The model predic-
tion is updated iteratively as follows:

Model evaluation
Fivefold cross-validation was used to guarantee the developed models’ generalizability 
and dependability. Five equal-sized subsets were randomly selected from the dataset. 
For each fold:
•	 Four subsets were used as the training data.
•	 The remaining subset was used as the testing data.
•	 This process was repeated five times, and the performance metrics were averaged 
across all folds.
To guarantee that every data point was used for both training and testing, the training 
and testing subsets were switched around in each iteration. By using this method, over-
fitting is reduced and reliable estimates of the model’s performance on unknown data 
are produced.

1.	 RMSE: RMSE measures the average magnitude of prediction errors, penalizing larger 
deviations.

Conclusions
This study developed and evaluated machine learning models to predict longitudinal 
cracking in CRCP using advanced techniques, including a PSO-optimized GBM model. 
The results demonstrated the superiority of the PSO-GBM model over baseline GBM 
and linear regression models, with the lowest mean RMSE (2.661) and the highest mean 
R2 (0.984) across fivefold cross-validation, highlighting its accuracy and robustness. 
The optimization process effectively tuned hyperparameters, such as NumLearningCy-
cles, LearnRate, and MaxNumSplits, to enhance predictive performance while avoiding 
overfitting.
Correlation analysis revealed significant relationships between longitudinal cracking 
and variables like age, KESAL, and initial IRI, while other factors, such as freeze index 
and precipitation, showed weaker correlations. The feature importance ranking iden-
tified L3 thickness, age, and AADTT as the most influential predictors, emphasizing 
the critical role of structural and traffic-related factors. Normalized sensitivity analysis

and actual values. Sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters confirmed the importance 
of careful tuning to achieve optimal performance and balance between complexity and 
generalization.
In conclusion, the PSO-GBM model offers a powerful tool for accurately predicting 
longitudinal cracking in CRCP, enabling transportation agencies to improve mainte-
nance strategies and optimize resource allocation. Future work could explore integrating 
additional environmental and material variables or applying the model to other forms 
of pavement distress to further enhance its applicability and effectiveness in real-world 
scenarios.
Limitations and future directions
Limitations
•	 Computational requirements: The PSO optimization process, while effective at 
enhancing predictive performance, is computationally demanding. Agencies without 
access to high-performance computing infrastructure may face challenges in imple-
menting the model for real-time applications.
•	 Model interpretability: Although gradient boosting machines (GBM) provide high 
accuracy, they are often considered “black-box” models. This limits transparency 
and may hinder practical adoption in agency workflows without the use of additional 
interpretability tools.
•	 Single-distress focus: This study focuses exclusively on predicting longitudinal crack-
ing. The model does not account for other common pavement distresses, such as 
transverse cracking, faulting, or rutting, which may limit its current utility for com-
prehensive pavement condition assessment.
•	 Pavement type scope: The model was developed and validated solely on data from 
continuously reinforced concrete pavement (CRCP). Therefore, its applicability to 
other pavement types has not been tested.
Future directions
•	 Adoption of cloud or batch computing: To overcome computational challenges, 
future implementations should explore cloud-based platforms or offline batch pro-
cessing to make the PSO-GBM model more accessible to agencies with limited com-
puting capacity.
•	 Integration of explainable AI: Incorporating interpretability frameworks, such as

Abstract: Longitudinal cracking poses a serious threat to the longevity and functionality of con‑ tinuously reinforced concrete pavement (CRCP). Using structural, traffic, and climatic data taken from the Long-Term Pavement Performance (LTPP) database, this study presents a machine learning system based on a gradient boosting machine (GBM) optimized using particle swarm optimization (PSO) to forecast longitudinal cracking. The proposed PSO-GBM model achieved the lowest mean RMSE (2.661) and highest R2 (0.984) across fivefold cross-validation, outperforming baseline GBM, linear regression, random forest, artificial neural networks (ANN), and support vector regression (SVR). Compared to traditional and untuned models, the PSO-GBM offers improved generali‑ zation and a stronger ability to capture nonlinear interactions among variables. Feature importance and sensitivity analyses identified L3 thickness, age, and AADTT as key pre‑ dictors. Despite the model’s exceptional predictive accuracy, computational demands and data availability may limit its practical application. However, the results offer useful information for transportation organizations looking to improve maintenance planning techniques and incorporate intelligent predictive tools into pavement management systems.
